newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia begins quiet regrets over leaks.
newsitem.headline: Australia begins quiet regrets over leaks.

text.p: CANBERRA, July 24 - Australia has refused to publicly apologise over a top secret paper slating Canberra's South Pacific allies, but has privately begun expressing regret to its neighbours over the insulting assessments.

Senior officials from New Zealand and the Cook Islands said Canberra had expressed regret over the AUSTEO (Australian Eyes Only) paper that made a scathing assessment of South Pacific economies and the foibles of some regional figures.
But New Zealand Minister of Maori Affairs Tau Henare demanded a public apology, calling the authors of the report and a second leaked AUSTEO paper "mongrels" and "noddy bureaucrats".
"I'm just basically wanting them, the Australians, to apologise," Henare told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
He described the first report's authors as "the pack of mongrels, and also I see there's another one been leaked by some noddy Australian bureaucrats".
New Zealand Foreign Minister Don McKinnon told Australian radio that Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer had already expressed regret over the first AUSTEO document.
"He did convey his apologies to the New Zealand government a few days ago," McKinnon said. "I certainly took that as being some contrition from Alexander."
New Zealand leaders have generally downplayed the AUSTEO paper's comments, saying they were embarrassing for Canberra but did not upset Wellington.
"Our meetings with them in future will be couched with a certain form of humour, I think," McKinnon said.

New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger, Treasurer Winston Peters -- described in the paper as a loose cannon and an opportunist -- and Finance Minister Bill Birch were due to leave for Australia on Thursday for talks with Australian leaders.

Australian High Commissioner to New Zealand Geoff Miller, who has responsibility for some Pacific nations, has told Cook Islands Prime Minister Geoffrey Henry that Canberra deeply regretted any embarrassment caused by the first report's release, Cook Islands officials said on Thursday.

The first AUSTEO document was a 93-page briefing to Treasurer Peter Costello for a summit of economic ministers from the 16-nation South Pacific Forum early this month in the tropical resort town of Cairns.
The second was a 39-page briefing for Costello for a series of bilateral talks following the summit.
Costello has rejected calls to apologise for the nature of the comments in the first report, but said they were insulting.
"I think when these sorts of things are published that they can be very deeply insulting," Costello said earlier this week.
Costello's department has asked one of the country's top intelligence chiefs to investigate the security breach that led to the two documents being obtained by journalists.
Both had been left on a hotel table in a public area at the economic ministers' conference.
